title: How Vietnam Became a Leading Mobile Gaming Market
summary: Discover how Vietnam evolved into one of the world's leading mobile gaming markets, from Flappy Bird to founder-led studios, hybrid-casual games, and global growth.
body_markdown:
Vietnam has become one of the world’s largest mobile game producers, yet many still underestimate both its studios and its domestic market. When people talk about mobile gaming, countries like China, Finland, and Turkey usually dominate the conversation. Vietnam rarely makes that list.


However, Vietnamese developers generated nearly 5 billion mobile game downloads, making the country[the second-largest exporter of mobile games by downloads.](https://tenjin.com/blog/vietnams-mobile-gaming-industry-5-trends/) At the same time, its domestic gaming market continues to grow, supported by a unique mix of local publishers, direct-to-consumer (D2C) payments, and a new generation of founder-led studios.


So, how did Vietnam get here?


In a recent episode of Tenjin ROI 101, Roman sat down with Maxon Pugovsky, Growth & Partnerships Lead at[Point to Web,](https://point2web.com/) to explore how Vietnam evolved from an outsourcing destination into one of the world’s most active mobile game ecosystems, and why many studios are only beginning to understand its potential.


## A Mobile Gaming Ecosystem Built by Founders


Many of today’s largest game development hubs have been shaped by venture capital. But, Vietnam has followed a different path. According to Maxon, many of the country’s successful studios were built by small teams that funded themselves instead of raising outside investment.


After the success of Flappy Bird, developers realized they didn’t need a large publisher or major investment to build a successful game.


> “People realized, ‘I can create my own company, release games, and make money.'”


That shift encouraged hundreds of developers to start their own studios. And, because operating costs were relatively low, founders could experiment, iterate, and have the freedom to grow it themselves, without immediately looking for investors. Even today, many successful studios remain independently owned.


As Maxon explained:


> “Most founders don’t dream about exiting. They want to keep building games.”


That long-term mindset has helped shape a resilient ecosystem. Instead of building companies for acquisition, many founders focus on creating sustainable businesses that continue to evolve over time.


## The Challenge Isn’t Downloads


Vietnam has already proven it can build games at scale. The next big challenge is building games that will trend to generate more value over their lifetime.


Historically, many Vietnamese studios found success through hypercasual games and advertising-driven business models. Those games delivered impressive download numbers, particularly across Android devices and emerging markets.


Today, the conversation is changing.


> “The Vietnamese industry understands that it needs to move beyond maximizing downloads and advertising revenue.”


Instead, studios are investing in deeper gameplay, stronger progression systems, and[more efficient monetization methods.](https://tenjin.com/blog/vietnam-mobile-gaming-d2c-payments/)


As Maxon put it:


> “The next step is building games with stronger monetization through in-app purchases, deeper gameplay, and long-term player engagement.”


This transition mirrors a broader trend across the entire mobile games industry. As user acquisition becomes more competitive, players tend to expect more enriching experiences, making long-term retention rates just as important as download volume.


## Beyond the Download Numbers


One of the biggest misconceptions about Vietnam is that it’s only a production hub. However, in reality, it’s also a growing consumer market.


Maxon explained that many international developers underestimate Vietnam because they only look at App Store and Google Play revenue. However, local payment systems and web shops account for the majority of transactions.


This means traditional app store data only tells part of the story. For studios evaluating new markets, understanding how players discover, purchase, and engage with games is just as important as understanding download numbers. It’s a reminder that market data should always be viewed in context.


## Building Relationships Matters


The discussion also highlighted something that isn’t captured in industry reports: culture.


For international studios interested in working with Vietnamese developers or publishers, understanding how business relationships are built can make collaboration much easier.


As Maxon explained:


> “Trust comes first. Business comes afterward.”


Relationships often develop before commercial discussions begin. That collaborative approach influences everything from partnerships to hiring and long-term business development. It’s just another example of why understanding a market means looking beyond the numbers.


## Why Vietnam Deserves More Attention


Vietnam’s mobile gaming industry is no longer defined by outsourcing alone. It’s home to founder-led studios, experienced development teams, growing investment, and an increasingly sophisticated approach to monetization.


For publishers, user acquisition teams, and developers, the market offers valuable lessons about sustainable growth, founder culture, and adapting to changing player behavior.


The industry’s next phase won’t simply be measured by downloads. It will be measured by stronger games, better player experiences, and more mature monetization strategies.


For anyone following the future of mobile gaming, Vietnam is a market worth watching.
